claim: The murine Trx1 system is dispensable for steady-state myeloid-cell hematopoiesis.
source: Here we show that in contrast to its critical role in T cells, the murine Trx1 system is dispensable for steady-state myeloid-cell hematopoiesis due to their capacity to tap the glutathione/glutaredoxin pathway for DNA biosynthesis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2 demonstrating normal myeloid cell numbers in Txnrd1-deficient mice.

claim: Myeloid cells can tap the glutathione/glutaredoxin pathway for DNA biosynthesis when the Trx1 system is absent.
source: Here we show that in contrast to its critical role in T cells, the murine Trx1 system is dispensable for steady-state myeloid-cell hematopoiesis due to their capacity to tap the glutathione/glutaredoxin pathway for DNA biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing that BSO treatment (which depletes GSH) in Txnrd1-deficient mice leads to loss of myeloid cells, indicating the GSH/Grx pathway compensates for Trx1 absence.

claim: The Trx1 pathway instrumentally enables nuclear NF-κB DNA-binding in monocytes and dendritic cells.
source: However, the Trx1 pathway instrumentally enables nuclear NF-κB DNA-binding and thereby pro-inflammatory responses in monocytes and dendritic cells.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 5D showing reduced NF-κB p65 binding to promoters of inflammatory genes in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs, and by ELISA-based DNA binding assays in Figure 5E.

claim: Trx1 is critical for NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β production in macrophages.
source: Moreover, independent of this activity, Trx1 is critical for NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β production in macrophages by detoxifying excessive ROS levels.
evidence: Figure 7A shows dramatically reduced IL-1β secretion in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs upon NLRP3 activation, and Figure 7B shows impaired caspase-1 processing.

claim: Trx1 regulates NLRP3 inflammasome activation by detoxifying excessive ROS levels.
source: Moreover, independent of this activity, Trx1 is critical for NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β production in macrophages by detoxifying excessive ROS levels.
evidence: Figure 7F-G shows increased ROS in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs, and Figure 7H-I demonstrates that catalase supplementation restores IL-1β production, indicating excessive ROS is the mechanism.

claim: Txnip is not involved as a redox-sensitive ligand of NLRP3.
source: Notably, we exclude the involvement of the Trx1 inhibitor Txnip as a redox-sensitive ligand of NLRP3 as previously proposed.
evidence: Figure 7K-M shows that Txnip-deficient BMDMs have normal IL-1β secretion and normal neutrophil infiltration in MSU-induced peritonitis, contradicting the previous proposal by Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: TAM injection into Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 mice completely abolished the development of T cells in the thymus.
source: TAM injection into Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 mice completely abolished the development of T cells in the thymus, leading to a massive reduction of CD4+CD8+ double positive, CD4+ and CD8+ single positive thymocytes (Figure 1A), as shown previously (Muri et al., 2018).
evidence: Figure 1A shows dramatic reduction in all thymocyte populations in Txnrd1-deficient mice compared to controls, and this is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: Numbers of eosinophils, neutrophils, monocytes and DCs were comparable in the bone marrow of TAM-treated Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 and control mice.
source: In striking contrast, numbers of eosinophils, neutrophils, monocytes and DCs were comparable in the bone marrow of TAM-treated Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 and control (Txnrd1fl/fl) mice (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating that the Trx1 system is dispensable for the process of hematopoiesis in these cells.
evidence: Figure 1B shows no significant differences in cell counts for these populations between Txnrd1-deficient and control mice.

claim: Monocytes, neutrophils and eosinophils were present in the blood with similar frequency in the absence and presence of Txnrd1.
source: Despite their short lifespan, monocytes, neutrophils and eosinophils were also present in the blood with a similar frequency in the absence and presence of Txnrd1 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Figure 1C shows comparable percentages of these cell types in blood between genotypes.

claim: Txnrd1 deficiency did not affect total numbers of alveolar macrophages, eosinophils, neutrophils, monocytes and conventional type 1 and 2 DCs in the lungs.
source: Moreover, Txnrd1 deficiency also did not affect total numbers of alveolar macrophages, eosinophils, neutrophils, monocytes and conventional type 1 and 2 DCs (cDC1 and cDC2) in the lungs (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Figure 1D shows no significant differences in these lung populations between Txnrd1-deficient and control mice.

claim: Myeloid populations in the spleen were unchanged in Txnrd1-deficient mice apart from a reduction in total numbers of cDC2.
source: Similarly, these populations were also unchanged in the spleen apart from a reduction in total numbers of cDC2 (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Figure 1E shows most splenic myeloid populations are unchanged, with only cDC2 showing a significant reduction.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient bone marrow completely failed to refill the T-cell compartment of irradiated recipients.
source: Expectedly, Txnrd1-deficient bone marrow completely failed to refill the T-cell compartment of irradiated recipients (Figure 1G), consistent with our previous findings reporting a crucial role of Trx1 for T-cell proliferation (Muri et al., 2018).
evidence: Figure 1G shows near-zero contribution of Txnrd1-deficient cells to T cell populations in chimeric mice, consistent with cited previous work.

claim: Eosinophils, neutrophils, monocytes, DCs and macrophages lacking Txnrd1 were reduced by 30–50% in competitive bone marrow chimeras.
source: Notably, eosinophils, neutrophils, monocytes, DCs and macrophages lacking Txnrd1 were reduced by 30–50% in the bone marrow, blood, spleen and lungs, as compared to WT counterparts, thus indicating a small contribution of Txnrd1 for the expansion of myeloid-cell precursors that could be revealed in a competitive situation with WT cells (Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), similar to B-cell development (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C; Muri et al., 2019b).
evidence: Figures 1H and 1I show 30-50% reduction in CD45.2+ (Txnrd1-deficient) myeloid cells compared to the expected 50% in competitive chimeras.

claim: BSO treatment significantly reduced total GSH levels in bone marrow and spleen.
source: Expectedly, BSO-treated mice showed a significant reduction in total GSH levels compared to controls in the bone marrow and in the spleen (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Figures 2B and 2C show statistically significant reduction in GSH levels after BSO treatment.

claim: GSH depletion by BSO strikingly reduced Txnrd1-deficient granulocytes within 5 days.
source: Interestingly, however, additional depletion of GSH strikingly reduced Txnrd1-deficient granulocytes within 5 days after oral BSO administration (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figures 2D and 2E show dramatic decline in CD45.2+ neutrophils and eosinophils after BSO treatment in Txnrd1-deficient chimeras.

claim: Oral administration of BSO to WT mice did not affect numbers of blood neutrophils and monocytes over time.
source: We further observed that oral administration of BSO to WT mice did not affect numbers of blood neutrophils and monocytes over time (Figure 2J).
evidence: Figure 2J shows stable neutrophil and monocyte percentages in WT mice treated with BSO.

claim: Numbers of various myeloid populations in bone marrow, spleen and lungs were not affected by GSH depletion in WT mice.
source: Moreover, the numbers of various myeloid populations in the bone marrow, spleen and lungs were not affected by GSH depletion in WT mice (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), therefore suggesting that the GSH/Grx system is only utilized as a backup system to compensate for the absence of the Trx1 pathway.
evidence: Figure 2K and supplement 2 show no significant changes in myeloid populations in WT mice after BSO treatment, supporting the interpretation that GSH/Grx is a backup system.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient mice displayed limited capacity to increase CD11b+Ly-6G-Ly-6Cint bone marrow precursors upon LPS administration.
source: While both groups of mice increased the numbers of CD11b+Ly-6G-Ly-6Cintbone marrow precursors upon LPS administration, Txnrd1-deficient mice displayed a limited capacity (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows significantly lower percentages of these precursors in Txnrd1-deficient mice after LPS treatment compared to controls.

claim: Accumulation of neutrophils in peripheral blood was impaired in Txnrd1-deficient mice during emergency hematopoiesis.
source: Moreover, accumulation of neutrophils in peripheral blood was also impaired in the absence of the Trx1 system (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Figures 3D and 3E show reduced neutrophil percentages in blood of Txnrd1-deficient mice after LPS-induced emergency hematopoiesis.

claim: Txnrd1 deletion was complete at the mRNA level in knockout BMDCs.
source: We first confirmed that Txnrd1 deletion was complete at the mRNA level in knockout BMDCs (Figure 4A) and that cell survival was not compromised (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4A shows near-zero Txnrd1 mRNA in Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 BMDCs compared to controls.

claim: Cell survival was not compromised in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.
source: We first confirmed that Txnrd1 deletion was complete at the mRNA level in knockout BMDCs (Figure 4A) and that cell survival was not compromised (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows similar viability percentages between Txnrd1-deficient and control BMDCs.

claim: Expression of Txn1 was upregulated upon TLR-driven stimulation in BMDCs.
source: Interestingly, expression of Txn1 was upregulated upon TLR-driven stimulation, potentially indicating an involvement of the Trx1 pathway in inflammatory responses (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows significantly increased Txn1 mRNA levels after stimulation with various TLR ligands.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs showed strikingly impaired production of IL-6, IL-12p40 and TNF-α in response to TLR stimuli.
source: Indeed, while WT BMDCs readily produced pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-12p40 and TNF-α in responses to each of the stimuli, this was strikingly impaired in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which was also evident at the transcriptional level (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Figures 4D, 4E, and supplement 1 show dramatically reduced cytokine secretion in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs, and Figures 4F-G show reduced mRNA levels.

claim: Secretion of IL-1β by TLR-primed BMDCs upon ATP, alum or nigericin stimulation was defective in the absence of Txnrd1.
source: Similarly, the secretion of IL-1β by TLR-primed BMDCs upon ATP, alum (Al(OH)3) or nigericin stimulation was also defective in the absence of Txnrd1 due to impaired transcription of the Il1b gene (Figure 4H,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 4H and supplement 2 show reduced IL-1β secretion, and Figure 4I shows reduced Il1b mRNA in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.

claim: Lower frequency of IFN-γ-producing CD4+ T cells was measured when naïve CD4+ T cells were co-cultured with Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.
source: Indeed, we measured a lower frequency of IFN-γ-producing CD4+ T cells when naïve CD4+ T cells were co-cultured with Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs (Figure 4J) compared to when they were co-cultured with WT controls.
evidence: Figure 4J shows significantly reduced percentages of IFN-γ+ CD4+ T cells in co-cultures with Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.

claim: TLR signaling was intact in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs upon stimulation with LPS or R837.
source: Interestingly, we observed intact TLR signaling in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs upon stimulation with LPS or R837, as assessed by the phosphorylation and consequent degradation of IκB-α and phosphorylation of Erk1/2 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), thus supporting the idea that early downstream events upon TLR stimulation are not affected by the absence of the Trx1 system.
evidence: Figure 5A and supplement 1 show similar patterns of IκB-α phosphorylation/degradation and Erk1/2 phosphorylation in Txnrd1-deficient and control BMDCs.

claim: No significant defects in nuclear translocation of NF-κB p65 were observed between Txnrd1-deficient and sufficient BMDCs.
source: However, we observed no significant defects in the nuclear translocation of NF-κB p65 between Txnrd1-deficient and sufficient BMDCs (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Figure 5B shows no significant difference in nuclear NF-κB signal between genotypes over time, and Figure 5C shows representative images.

claim: Reduced NF-κB p65 DNA binding to the promoters of Il12b, Il1b, Il6, and Nfkbia was observed in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.
source: In keeping with our hypothesis, we observed reduced NF-κB p65 DNA binding to the promoters of the pro-inflammatory genes Il12b, Il1b and Il6, and of the notorious NF-κB target gene Nfkbia (encoding IκB-α) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows significantly reduced ChIP signal for p65 at these promoters in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.

claim: NF-κB p65 transcription factor DNA binding in nuclear extracts was reduced in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.
source: Furthermore, we validated our ChIP results using an ELISA-based method for detecting specific p65 transcription factor DNA binding in nuclear extracts (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows significantly reduced p65 DNA binding activity in Txnrd1-deficient BMDC nuclear extracts.

claim: Txnrd1 deficiency resulted in a significant increase in total cellular ROS levels in BMDCs.
source: Despite a significant increase in total cellular ROS levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), the reduction in IL-12p40 secretion by Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs was not restored by the supplementation of a panel of antioxidants (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Figure 5 supplement 3A shows significantly higher ROS levels in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs after LPS stimulation.

claim: Reduction in IL-12p40 secretion by Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs was not restored by supplementation of antioxidants.
source: Despite a significant increase in total cellular ROS levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), the reduction in IL-12p40 secretion by Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs was not restored by the supplementation of a panel of antioxidants (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Figure 5 supplement 3B-C show that various antioxidants (NAC, AA, DTT, DPI, catalase) did not restore IL-12p40 secretion in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.

claim: Expression of Txnrd1 and Txn1 was increased in M1 compared to M2 macrophages.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased expression of Txnrd1 and Txn1 in M1 compared to M2 macrophages and in BMDMs stimulated with a variety of TLR ligands (Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), consistent with a possible role in maintaining redox homeostasis in ROS-generating M1 macrophages; however, no difference in expression of the Trx1 system inhibitor Txnip was detected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figures 6B-C show significantly higher Txnrd1 and Txn1 mRNA in M1 vs M2 macrophages.

claim: Lower expression of M1 markers Nos2, Cd38, Hif1a and Gpr18 was observed in M1-polarized Txnrd1-deficient cells.
source: In keeping with the induction of the Trx1 system in M1 macrophages, we observed lower expression of the M1 markers Nos2, Cd38, Hif1a and Gpr18 in M1-polarized Txnrd1-deficient cells compared to the WT controls (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Figure 6D and supplements show significantly reduced expression of these M1 markers in Txnrd1-deficient M1 macrophages.

claim: Txnrd1 deletion did not affect M2 polarization as measured by M2 markers.
source: However, Txnrd1 deletion did not affect M2 polarization as measured by the RNA expression of the known M2 markers Fizz1, Arg1 and Ym1 (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G), and protein levels of Relmα, CD301b, PDL2 and CD206 (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: Figure 6F-G and supplements show no significant differences in M2 markers between Txnrd1-deficient and control M2 macrophages.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient and sufficient BMDMs underwent cell death to a similar extent during M1 polarization.
source: Importantly, we excluded that defective M1 polarization was a consequence of cell death, since Txnrd1-deficient and sufficient BMDMs underwent cell death to a similar extent (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Figure 6H and supplement 1K show no significant differences in viability or LDH release between genotypes during M1 polarization.

claim: IL-12p40 levels remained unaffected in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs stimulated with TLR ligands.
source: To our surprise and in striking contrast to the results obtained with BMDCs, IL-12p40 levels remained unaffected (Figure 6I), while production of IL-6 (Figure 6J) and TNF-α (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) was even increased in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs compared to controls.
evidence: Figure 6I shows no significant differences in IL-12p40 secretion between Txnrd1-deficient and control BMDMs.

claim: Production of IL-6 and TNF-α was increased in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs compared to controls.
source: To our surprise and in striking contrast to the results obtained with BMDCs, IL-12p40 levels remained unaffected (Figure 6I), while production of IL-6 (Figure 6J) and TNF-α (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) was even increased in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs compared to controls.
evidence: Figure 6J and supplement 2 show significantly higher IL-6 and TNF-α secretion in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs.

claim: All Grx isoforms were higher expressed in BMDM compared to BMDC cultures.
source: Interestingly, we observed that all Grx isoforms were higher expressed in BMDM compared to BMDC cultures (Figure 6N).
evidence: Figure 6N shows significantly higher expression of Grx1, Grx2, Grx3, and Grx5 in BMDMs compared to BMDCs.

claim: Treatment of Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs with BSO drastically reduced IL-12p40 secretion.
source: Treatment of Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 BMDMs with BSO drastically reduced IL-12p40 secretion to minimal levels (Figure 6O and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), without affecting viability (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Figure 6O shows dramatically reduced IL-12p40 in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs treated with BSO.

claim: BSO treatment did not affect cytokine secretion by WT BMDMs.
source: In addition, BSO‐treatment did not affect cytokine secretion by WT BMDMs (Figure 6O and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that the Trx1 system alone is sufficient for sustaining cytokine production.
evidence: Figure 6O shows no significant change in IL-12p40 secretion in WT BMDMs with BSO treatment, supporting the interpretation.

claim: NF-κB p65 DNA binding activity was not affected by Txnrd1 deletion in BMDMs.
source: In keeping with no decrease in IL-6, IL-12p40 and TNF-α secretion in the absence of the Trx1 system, we observed that NF-κB p65 DNA binding activity was not affected by Txnrd1 deletion (Figure 6P).
evidence: Figure 6P shows no significant difference in p65 DNA binding between Txnrd1-deficient and control BMDMs without BSO treatment.

claim: Blocking the GSH/Grx pathway by BSO treatment in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs completely abrogated the DNA-binding capacity of NF-κB p65.
source: Interestingly, however, blocking the GSH/Grx pathway by BSO treatment in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs turned out to completely abrogate the DNA-binding capacity of NF-κB p65, thereby confirming the compensatory activity of the GSH/Grx system in BMDMs (Figure 6P).
evidence: Figure 6P shows dramatically reduced p65 DNA binding in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs treated with BSO.

claim: Release of mature IL-1β induced by NLRP3 activators was abrogated in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, release of mature IL-1β induced by the NLRP3 activators ATP and alum following priming with various TLR ligands was abrogated in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) as shown using an ELISA assay known to display a much higher sensitivity for mature IL-1β than for its pro-form (Dick et al., 2016).
evidence: Figure 7A and supplement 1A show dramatically reduced IL-1β secretion in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs upon NLRP3 activation, with citation supporting the ELISA specificity.

claim: Processing of caspase-1 to its active form was dramatically impaired in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs.
source: Consistent with a defective NLRP3 inflammasome, the processing of caspase-1 to its active form was also dramatically impaired (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 7B and supplement 1B show reduced cleaved caspase-1 (p10) in supernatants of Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs.

claim: Levels of pro-IL-1β in cell lysates and transcription of Il1b mRNA were unaffected in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs upon TLR priming.
source: This was additionally confirmed by western blotting showing strikingly reduced release of processed IL-1β upon NLRP3 inflammasome activation, while levels of pro-IL-1β in cell lysates (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and transcription of Il1b mRNA were unaffected in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs upon TLR priming (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7B shows similar pro-IL-1β levels in cell lysates, and Figure 7C shows no significant difference in Il1b mRNA between genotypes.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient mice display impaired neutrophil influx upon MSU injection.
source: In line with the in vitro defects, we found that Txnrd1-deficient mice display an impaired neutrophil influx (Figure 7D) and reduced IL-1β production (Figure 7E) upon MSU injection compared to WT mice.
evidence: Figure 7D shows significantly fewer neutrophils in peritoneal lavage of Txnrd1-deficient mice after MSU treatment.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient mice display reduced IL-1β production upon MSU injection.
source: In line with the in vitro defects, we found that Txnrd1-deficient mice display an impaired neutrophil influx (Figure 7D) and reduced IL-1β production (Figure 7E) upon MSU injection compared to WT mice.
evidence: Figure 7E shows significantly lower IL-1β levels in peritoneal lavage of Txnrd1-deficient mice after MSU treatment.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs accumulated ROS to a higher extent compared to control cells after treatment with LPS or R837.
source: To test this possibility, we first quantified cellular ROS in the absence of the Trx1 system by CM-H2DCFDA staining and observed that Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs accumulated ROS to a higher extent compared to control cells after treatment with LPS or R837 (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: Figures 7F-G show significantly higher ROS levels (MFI) in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs after LPS or R837 stimulation.

claim: Supplementation with catalase restored ATP- and alum-induced IL-1β production in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs up to WT levels.
source: Notably, we additionally found that supplementation with a cell-permeable version of catalase, one of the main cellular antioxidants involved in the neutralization of hydrogen peroxide, can restore ATP- and alum-induced IL-1β production in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs up to WT levels (Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 7H and supplement 2 show that catalase treatment restores IL-1β secretion in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs to levels comparable to WT.

claim: Addition of catalase does not affect the expression of the Il1b gene.
source: As a control, we verified that addition of catalase does not affect the expression of the Il1b gene (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 7 supplement 3 shows no significant difference in Il1b mRNA with catalase treatment.

claim: Other classical antioxidants (NAC, AA, DTT, DPI) did not rescue impaired IL-1β production in the absence of the Trx1 system.
source: By contrast, other classical antioxidants, such as N-acetyl-L-cysteine (NAC), ascorbic acid (AA), dithiothreitol (DTT), and diphenyleneiodonium (DPI), did not rescue the impaired IL-1β production in the absence of the Trx1 system (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 7 supplement 4 shows that these antioxidants did not restore IL-1β secretion in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs.

claim: Only low concentrations of catalase restored defective IL-1β production in Txnrd1-deficient cells.
source: We observed that only low concentrations of catalase restored defective IL-1β production in Txnrd1-deficient cells (Figure 7I) and concomitantly reduced ROS to levels observed in WT cells (Figure 7J).
evidence: Figure 7I shows that low catalase restores IL-1β in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs, while Figure 7J shows corresponding ROS reduction to WT levels.

claim: Higher concentrations of catalase more potently inhibited cellular ROS and consequently IL-1β secretion upon NLRP3 inflammasome activation in both WT and Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs.
source: However, higher concentrations of the antioxidant catalase (described as 'medium' and 'high' in the graphs) more potently inhibited cellular ROS and consequently IL-1β secretion upon NLRP3 inflammasome activation in both WT and Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs (Figure 7I,J), in line with the general view of ROS as triggers of the NLRP3 inflammasome (Tschopp and Schroder, 2010).
evidence: Figures 7I-J show that medium and high catalase concentrations reduce both ROS and IL-1β in both genotypes, with citation supporting the ROS-NLRP3 connection.

claim: Txnip deletion was complete at the mRNA level in Txnip-deficient BMDMs.
source: Although Txnip deletion was complete at the mRNA level (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A), Txnip-deficient BMDMs did not show any defects in IL-12p40 (Figure 7—figure supplement 5B) and IL-1β secretion (Figure 7K,L and Figure 7—figure supplement 5C) compared to WT controls.
evidence: Figure 7 supplement 5A shows near-zero Txnip mRNA in Txnipfl/fl;Vav1-Cre BMDMs.

claim: Txnip-deficient BMDMs did not show defects in IL-12p40 and IL-1β secretion compared to WT controls.
source: Although Txnip deletion was complete at the mRNA level (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A), Txnip-deficient BMDMs did not show any defects in IL-12p40 (Figure 7—figure supplement 5B) and IL-1β secretion (Figure 7K,L and Figure 7—figure supplement 5C) compared to WT controls.
evidence: Figure 7 supplement 5B shows no significant difference in IL-12p40, and Figures 7K-L and supplement 5C show no significant differences in IL-1β secretion between Txnip-deficient and control BMDMs.

claim: Administration of MSU into Txnip-deficient and sufficient mice elicited a comparable influx of neutrophils in the peritoneum.
source: Moreover, administration of MSU into Txnip-deficient and sufficient mice elicited a comparable influx of neutrophils in the peritoneum (Figure 7M), thereby further supporting the dispensability of Txnip in NLRP3 inflammasome activation.
evidence: Figure 7M shows no significant difference in neutrophil counts in peritoneal lavage between Txnip-deficient and control mice after MSU treatment.

claim: The Trx and GSH/Grx systems are the two main pathways that make up the cellular redox system.
source: The two main pathways that make up this cellular redox system are the thioredoxin (Trx) system and the glutathione (GSH) system (Arnér and Holmgren, 2000; Couto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Both the Trx and GSH systems ultimately rely on the reducing power from NADPH.
source: Both the Trx and GSH systems ultimately rely on the reducing power from NADPH, which in mammals is generated by the alternative oxidation of glucose in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) (Stanton, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: NADPH in mammals is generated by the alternative oxidation of glucose in the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: Both the Trx and GSH systems ultimately rely on the reducing power from NADPH, which in mammals is generated by the alternative oxidation of glucose in the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) (Stanton, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The Trx and GSH/Grx systems provide reducing equivalents for DNA synthesis by ribonucleotide reductase during proliferation.
source: For instance, they fuel the reducing power for DNA synthesis by ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) during proliferation, for scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), and for the reduction of protein disulfides back to their reduced state (Camier et al., 2007; Holmgren, 1985; Holmgren, 2000; Muri et al., 2018; Potamitou et al., 2002; Prinz et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Macrophages and dendritic cells secrete several inflammatory cytokines to orchestrate immune responses.
source: Macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs) secrete several inflammatory cytokines to orchestrate immune responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field of immunology.

claim: Upon sensing microbial components via TLRs, macrophages and DCs utilize the MyD88 adaptor to activate NF-κB-dependent transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Upon sensing microbial components via Toll-like receptors (TLR), they utilize the MyD88 adaptor to activate nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB)-dependent transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-6 (encoded by the Il6 gene), IL-12p40 (encoded by the Il12b gene), TNF-α (encoded by the Tnfa gene) and IL-1β (encoded by the Il1b gene) (Akira and Takeda, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Secretion of IL-1β needs a second signal required for inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation.
source: Secretion of IL-1β, however, needs a second signal required for inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 or −11 activation, processing of the immature IL-1β precursor (pro-IL-1β), and subsequent release of the active and mature form of IL-1β (Martinon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Cellular redox regulation and ROS production have been described to regulate both NF-κB activity and NLRP3 inflammasome function.
source: Interestingly, cellular redox regulation and ROS production have been described to regulate both NF-κB activity (Morgan and Liu, 2011) and NLRP3 inflammasome function (Tschopp and Schroder, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Txnip has been proposed to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to ROS.
source: In particular, the Trx-inhibitor Txnip has been proposed to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to ROS (Zhou et al., 2010), although these results remain controversial (Masters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a previous proposal in the literature with citations, though noted as controversial.

claim: The Trx1 system is critically required to fuel reducing power for DNA biosynthesis during metabolic reprogramming in T but not in follicular B cells.
source: Notably, we demonstrated that the Trx1 system is critically required to fuel reducing power for the sustainment of DNA biosynthesis during metabolic reprogramming in T but not in follicular B cells (Muri et al., 2018; Muri et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors with supporting citations.

claim: Trx1 provides reducing equivalents for the redox-dependent binding of NF-κB p65 to target DNA in DCs.
source: Using BMDCs, we showed that Trx1 provides reducing equivalents for the redox-dependent binding of the NF-κB p65 transcription factor to target DNA in DCs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Redox regulation of NF-κB activity by the Trx1 antioxidant pathway has been proposed, but its contribution in inflammation remains controversial.
source: Interestingly, while redox regulation of NF-κB activity by the Trx1 antioxidant pathway has been proposed, its contribution in inflammation remains controversial because both activating and inhibitory effects have been described (Isakov et al., 2014; Kabe et al., 2005; Lillig and Holmgren, 2007; Morgan and Liu, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as existing controversy in the literature with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The Trx1 system promotes NF-κB DNA binding probably by structural modification of a component of the NF-κB binding complex.
source: Trx1 promotes NF-κB DNA binding probably by structural modification of a component(s) (e.g. via reduction of disulfide bonds) of the NF-κB binding complex rather than through indirect effects of ROS, since supplementation with different antioxidants did not restore NF-κB activity in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data showing antioxidants don't rescue the phenotype, suggesting a direct redox mechanism.

claim: GM-CSF-driven BMDCs comprise a mixture of conventional DCs, monocyte-derived DCs and macrophages.
source: GM-CSF-driven BMDCs are known to comprise a mixture of conventional DCs, monocyte-derived DCs and macrophages (Helft et al., 2015), with the latter population only capable of inflammasome-dependent IL-1β production (Erlich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Only macrophages in BMDC cultures are capable of inflammasome-dependent IL-1β production.
source: GM-CSF-driven BMDCs are known to comprise a mixture of conventional DCs, monocyte-derived DCs and macrophages (Helft et al., 2015), with the latter population only capable of inflammasome-dependent IL-1β production (Erlich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: BMDMs generated with M-CSF consist of a pure population of macrophages.
source: Therefore, we aimed to verify our results in BMDMs generated with M-CSF, which are thought to consist of a pure population of macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale based on established understanding in the field.

claim: BMDMs have higher expression of cellular Grx proteins compared to BMDCs.
source: Indeed, we showed that BMDMs but not BMDCs have the capability to engage the Grx pathway when the Trx1 system is genetically deleted. Thus, Trx1 activates NF-κB transcription, and depending on the expression levels of Grx proteins in different myeloid-cell types, Txnrd1-deficiency may have more or less pronounced outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6N showing higher Grx expression in BMDMs.

claim: Myeloid cells generate high amounts of ROS by NADPH oxidases to fight intracellular microbes.
source: Myeloid cells are known to generate high amounts of ROS by NADPH oxidases to fight intracellular microbes, which may explain the requirement of robust ROS scavenging systems (Lambeth, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: NLRP3-dependent IL-1β production in macrophages is independent of Txnip both in vitro and in vivo.
source: In contrast, our study identifies the Txnip-interacting partner Trx1 as a critical regulator of inflammasome-dependent IL-1β release in macrophages. In the absence of the Trx1 system, we observed drastically impaired IL-1β production in response to classical NLRP3 stimuli in vitro and during MSU-induced peritonitis in vivo, while pro-Il1b transcription was unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7K-M showing normal IL-1β production and neutrophil infiltration in Txnip-deficient mice.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs displayed excessive intracellular ROS levels upon TLR triggering.
source: Interestingly, Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs displayed excessive intracellular ROS levels upon TLR triggering, and decomposition of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen with a cell-permeable form of the enzyme catalase restored IL-1β production.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 7F-G showing increased ROS, and Figures 7H-I showing catalase rescue.

claim: Moderate ROS levels act as triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that moderate ROS levels act as triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome in line with the known role of mitochondrial ROS released from stressed mitochondria (Latz et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2011), while excessive ROS levels display an opposite effect and inhibit NLRP3 activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing hormetic ROS effects, with citations supporting the role of mitochondrial ROS.

claim: Excessive ROS levels inhibit NLRP3 activation.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that moderate ROS levels act as triggers for the NLRP3 inflammasome in line with the known role of mitochondrial ROS released from stressed mitochondria (Latz et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2011), while excessive ROS levels display an opposite effect and inhibit NLRP3 activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data showing that high catalase (which reduces ROS more) inhibits IL-1β in both WT and KO cells (Figure 7I-J).

claim: ROS must be kept within a restricted window of concentrations to allow inflammasome activation.
source: Taken together, ROS must be kept within a restricted window of concentrations to allow inflammasome activation, where both an excess or an undersupply prevent it.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the hormetic dose-response relationship observed in the data.

claim: The regulation of NLRP3 inflammasome activity by ROS follows a hormetic pattern.
source: A non-linear dose response to a stressor (e.g. ROS) with a certain effect at low doses and the reverse at high doses has been referred to as hormesis (Ristow, 2014; Ristow and Schmeisser, 2011). Our results are in line with an hormetic regulation of NLRP3 inflammasome activity by ROS, which promote its assembly at moderate concentrations, while they inhibit it at low and high concentrations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citations defining hormesis.

claim: M1 macrophages are associated with inflammatory responses.
source: While classically activated M1 macrophages are associated with inflammatory responses, alternatively activated M2 macrophages are described as anti-inflammatory, thereby promoting tissue remodeling and resolution of inflammation (Chinetti-Gbaguidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: M2 macrophages are anti-inflammatory and promote tissue remodeling and resolution of inflammation.
source: While classically activated M1 macrophages are associated with inflammatory responses, alternatively activated M2 macrophages are described as anti-inflammatory, thereby promoting tissue remodeling and resolution of inflammation (Chinetti-Gbaguidi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: M1 macrophages undergo increased rates of glycolysis compared to M2 macrophages.
source: For instance, M1 macrophages undergo increased rates of glycolysis compared to M2 macrophages, allowing rapid ATP production and sustainment of the PPP in order to generate NADPH for ROS production and de novo nucleotide biosynthesis (Kelly and O'Neill, 2015; O'Neill, 2015; Russell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: LPS/IFN-γ but not IL-4 stimulation leads to induction of the Trx1 system.
source: We found that LPS/IFN-γ but not IL-4 stimulation leads to an induction of the Trx1 system, which is in line with the observed impairment in M1 polarization in the absence of the Trx1 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6B-C showing increased Txnrd1 and Txn1 in M1 but not M2 conditions.

claim: Trx1 donates electrons to RNR, which catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the PPP leading to nucleotide biosynthesis.
source: As discussed above, Trx1 donates electrons to RNR, which catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the PPP, leading to nucleotide biosynthesis (Holmgren and Sengupta, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: M2 macrophages suppress the PPP.
source: M2 macrophages, on the other hand, seem to suppress the PPP (Haschemi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Targeting Trx1 may be exploited to treat inflammatory diseases.
source: Together, this study suggests that targeting Trx1 may be exploited to treat inflammatory diseases.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the overall findings showing Trx1's role in inflammation.

claim: Cre-mediated deletion in total bone marrow cells and in CD11b+ splenocytes of Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 mice was complete at the genomic DNA and mRNA levels.
source: Cre-mediated deletion in total bone marrow cells and in CD11b+ splenocytes of Txnrd1fl/fl;Rosa26-CreERT2 mice was complete at the genomic DNA and mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 1 supplement 1 shows near-complete loss of Txnrd1 DNA and mRNA in these cells.

claim: Txnrd1-deficient tissue resident macrophages in the lungs and spleen showed only a minor reduction upon BSO administration.
source: Although DCs were similarly affected, Txnrd1-deficient tissue resident macrophages in the lungs and in the spleen only showed a minor reduction upon BSO administration, consistent with their fetal origin and local persistence by slow turnover during adult life (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: Figures 2G-H show smaller reductions in macrophages compared to other myeloid cells, with interpretation based on known biology of tissue-resident macrophages.

claim: Tissue resident macrophages have fetal origin and persist locally by slow turnover during adult life.
source: Although DCs were similarly affected, Txnrd1-deficient tissue resident macrophages in the lungs and in the spleen only showed a minor reduction upon BSO administration, consistent with their fetal origin and local persistence by slow turnover during adult life (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge used to interpret the data.

claim: The GSH/Grx pathway does not efficiently compensate for the absence of the Trx1 system during emergency hematopoiesis.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that the GSH/Grx pathway does not efficiently compensate for the absence of the Trx1 system during emergency hematopoiesis when massive proliferation occurs due to LPS stress.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data in Figure 3 showing impaired emergency myelopoiesis in Txnrd1-deficient mice.

claim: The defect in expansion during emergency hematopoiesis was comparable to the one shown in competitive chimera settings.
source: The observed defect in expansion was therefore comparable to the one shown in competitive chimera settings.
evidence: This is a comparison between the emergency hematopoiesis data (Figure 3) and the chimera data (Figure 1).

claim: The absence of the Trx1 system in BMDCs inhibits their capacity to induce pro-inflammatory, IFN-γ-producing Th1 cells.
source: Therefore, the absence of the Trx1 system in BMDCs inhibits their capacity to induce pro-inflammatory, IFN-γ-producing Th1 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data in Figure 4J showing reduced Th1 polarization by Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs.

claim: IL-12 plays an important role in the polarization of T helper type 1 (Th1) cells.
source: Considering the important role of IL-12 in the polarization of T helper type 1 (Th1) cells (Langenkamp et al., 2000), we next wondered whether reduced IL-12 production by Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs would affect their ability to drive Th1 polarization of CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: TLR associate with adaptor molecules such as MyD88 to activate the IKK complex and mitogen-activated protein kinases upon binding of microbial ligands.
source: Upon binding of microbial ligands, TLR associate with adaptor molecules such as MyD88 to activate the IKK complex and mitogen-activated protein kinases, such as extracellular receptor kinase (Erk), p38 and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), which in turn influence the activity of the transcription factors NF-κB, AP1 and CREB, thereby ultimately regulating expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Akira and Takeda, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Early downstream events upon TLR stimulation are not affected by the absence of the Trx1 system.
source: Interestingly, we observed intact TLR signaling in Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs upon stimulation with LPS or R837, as assessed by the phosphorylation and consequent degradation of IκB-α and phosphorylation of Erk1/2 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), thus supporting the idea that early downstream events upon TLR stimulation are not affected by the absence of the Trx1 system.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on western blot data showing normal signaling patterns.

claim: Proteolysis of IκB-α results in the release and translocation of NF-κB p65 and p50 to the nucleus.
source: Proteolysis of IκB-α results in the release and translocation of NF-κB p65 and p50 to the nucleus, where it induces the transcription of genes encoding pro-inflammatory cytokines (Akira and Takeda, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Txnrd1 deficiency does not affect the nuclear translocation of NF-κB p65.
source: Overall, the microscopy analysis demonstrates that Txnrd1 deficiency does not affect the nuclear translocation of NF-κB p65, therefore suggesting a downstream defect.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on microscopy data in Figures 5B-C.

claim: The defect in pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion is not a consequence of a general increase of ROS but is due to compromised Trx1-mediated regulation of the redox status of NF-κB.
source: Together, these results suggest that the defect in pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion is not a consequence of a general increase of ROS but is due to the compromised Trx1-mediated regulation of the redox status of NF-κB, which interferes with NF-κB p65 binding to the DNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the failure of antioxidants to rescue the phenotype and the ChIP/DNA binding data.

claim: The BMDC culture comprises both conventional DCs and monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: The BMDC culture is known to comprise both conventional DCs and monocyte-derived macrophages (Helft et al., 2015) with the latter only possessing the capacity of inflammasome activation and IL-1β release (Erlich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: BMDMs can utilize both the Trx1 and GSH/Grx systems to fuel redox reactions for promoting NF-κB-binding activity.
source: Overall, here we show that while BMDCs are critically dependent on the Trx1 system for NF-κB-mediated pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, BMDMs can utilize both the Trx1 and GSH/Grx systems to fuel redox reactions aimed at promoting NF-κB-binding activity and consequent transcription of pro-inflammatory target genes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data showing normal NF-κB activity in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs (Figure 6P) that is lost with BSO treatment.

claim: An intact signal one in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs allowed study of signal two and inflammasome activation.
source: An intact signal one in Txnrd1-deficient BMDMs, in contrast to Txnrd1-deficient BMDCs, allowed us to study the quality of signal two and inflammasome activation in the absence of Txnrd1.
evidence: This is a rationale statement explaining why BMDMs were used to study inflammasome function.

claim: The Trx1 system promotes NLRP3 inflammasome activation and consequently secretion of mature IL-1β.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that the Trx1 system promotes NLRP3 inflammasome activation and consequently secretion of the mature IL-1β.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data in Figure 7A-C showing impaired IL-1β processing and secretion.

claim: The Trx1 system is a major player in the control of cellular antioxidant responses.
source: The Trx1 system is a major player in the control of cellular antioxidant responses (Mustacich and Powis, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The Trx1 pathway is crucial for IL-1β production in macrophages by prevention of excessive accumulation of hydrogen peroxide.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that the Trx1 pathway is crucial for IL-1β production in macrophages by prevention of an excessive accumulation of hydrogen peroxide.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data showing increased ROS (Figure 7F-G) and catalase rescue (Figure 7H-I).

claim: Excessive levels of ROS may lead to oxidation of particular components of the inflammasome machinery with detrimental consequences for their ability to assemble and/or cleave IL-1β.
source: Excessive ROS concentrations may lead to the oxidation of particular components of the inflammasome machinery (e.g. ASC, NLRP3, or caspase-1), with detrimental consequences for their ability to assemble and/or cleave IL-1β.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed inhibition by excessive ROS.

claim: Nitrogen oxide (NO) has been reported to induce NLRP3 and caspase-1 nitrosylation and thereby inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activity.
source: In keeping with this hypothesis, nitrogen oxide (NO) has been reported to induce NLRP3 and caspase-1 nitrosylation and thereby inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activity (Kim et al., 1998; Mishra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence from the literature with citations.

claim: The importance of the Trx1 system in M1 polarization is consistent with the high rates of the PPP in these cells.
source: Therefore, the importance of the Trx1 system in M1 polarization is consistent with the high rates of the PPP in these cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the observed M1 defect with known M1 metabolism.

claim: M1 macrophages may need high amounts of DNA building blocks to generate different RNA populations such as microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs.
source: Why M1 macrophages require such enormous amounts of DNA building blocks despite their low proliferative capacity is unknown, although it has been suggested that they need them to generate different RNA populations, such as microRNAs and long non-coding RNAs (O'Neill et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation from the literature with a citation.

claim: The differential redox regulation in BMDCs and BMDMs may reflect distinct requirements of the Trx1 and GSH/Grx pathways for inflammatory responses of different myeloid cell types in vivo.
source: The differential redox regulation in BMDCs and BMDMs may reflect distinct requirements of the Trx1 and GSH/Grx pathways for the inflammatory response of DCs, tissue macrophages and monocyte-derived macrophages in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the in vitro findings for in vivo relevance.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of MSU elicits NLRP3-dependent production of mature IL-1β in mouse peritoneum leading to massive infiltration of neutrophils.
source: Intraperitoneal administration of monosodium urate (MSU) is well known to elicit NLRP3-dependent production of mature IL-1β in mouse peritoneum leading to a massive infiltration of neutrophils (Martinon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.
